# 🧰 Command reference

Every command of `pasture <group> <command>`, with its safety level. The same
text is in the terminal: `pasture help`, `pasture help <group> <command>`, and
`pasture list --json` for agents.

**Safety levels.** `read` only reads. `write` changes local state and has
`--dry-run`. `external` touches other systems: it prints its plan and exits 3
unless given `--yes`, so an agent shows the plan and asks you first.

**Exit codes**, shared by every command: 0 ok, 1 failed, 2 usage, 3 needs you,
4 timed out, 5 missing tool.

| Command | Safety | Does |
| ------- | ------ | ---- |
| [`pasture agent ask`](#pasture-agent-ask) | write | Send one prompt to another agent, wait for it to settle, print its answer |
| [`pasture agent ps`](#pasture-agent-ps) | read | What each agent is really running — process tree, open servers, outbound — before you stop it |
| [`pasture agent stop`](#pasture-agent-stop) | external | Stop an agent without waiting for it to cooperate — graceful, then forced |
| [`pasture agent sweep`](#pasture-agent-sweep) | external | Free memory — send idle agents home, keep a ledger to call them back |
| [`pasture dep audit`](#pasture-dep-audit) | read | Scan this repo offline for secrets, SAST issues, and vulnerable deps |
| [`pasture dep cve`](#pasture-dep-cve) | read | Look up one dependency or CVE: is this lib vulnerable, how risky is this CVE |
| [`pasture doc review`](#pasture-doc-review) | external | Fresh-eyes review of a doc — each reviewer a NEW headless agent (no shared context), several vendors |
| [`pasture flow board`](#pasture-flow-board) | read | SDLC pipeline board — what lifecycle stage every agent's task sits at |
| [`pasture git guard`](#pasture-git-guard) | read | Pre-push gate — block a push to a PUBLIC remote that carries a secret |
| [`pasture git protect`](#pasture-git-protect) | write | Install the pre-push secret guard into this repo (keeps any existing hook) |
| [`pasture git visibility`](#pasture-git-visibility) | read | Ask the forge whether a git remote is public, private, or internal |
| [`pasture mr fanout`](#pasture-mr-fanout) | external | Move stacked branches off the branch below them and onto the default branch (trunk-based) |
| [`pasture mr stack`](#pasture-mr-stack) | read | Show open merge requests as a stack: what sits on what, own vs cumulative diff, CI |
| [`pasture pane tail`](#pasture-pane-tail) | read | Read another pane's recent output, or wait until a pattern shows up |
| [`pasture repo who`](#pasture-repo-who) | read | Which agents stand in which worktree of this repo — look before you code here |
| [`pasture sec pentest`](#pasture-sec-pentest) | external | Pentest your own code or local app with Strix AI agents, inside its Docker sandbox |
| [`pasture stack attach`](#pasture-stack-attach) | write | Put git's HEAD back on this worktree's branch after Sapling detached it |
| [`pasture stack push`](#pasture-stack-push) | external | Push each commit of the current Sapling stack to its own branch, optionally as a chain of MRs |
| [`pasture sys line`](#pasture-sys-line) | read | One-line machine load + memory metric with trend sparklines (for a status line) |
| [`pasture web read`](#pasture-web-read) | read | Read a web page as text: plain fetch first, a real browser when that fails |

## agent

### pasture agent ask

Send one prompt to another agent, wait for it to settle, print its answer

- **Safety:** `write`
- **Usage:** `pasture agent ask <name|pane> "<prompt>" [--timeout SECONDS] [--lines N] [--json] [--dry-run]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/agent/ask`](../cmds/agent/ask)

```text
Checks the agent first and never talks over it:
  blocked  → exit 3: it waits for the user; report it, never answer it
  working  → waits for it to finish first (same timeout)
Then submits the prompt, waits for idle/done/blocked and prints the last
--lines (default 200) of its output. Exit 3 if it ends blocked, 4 on timeout.
```

### pasture agent ps

What each agent is really running — process tree, open servers, outbound — before you stop it

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture agent ps <pane|--all> [--json]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/agent/ps`](../cmds/agent/ps)

```text
A pre-stop recon snapshot. herdr's idle/done tells you the AGENT settled, not
whether it left a server or build running. This joins four layers:
  herdr agent  → status, worktree (cwd), branch
  pane procs   → the agent root pid + its MCP children (herdr foreground group)
  OS tree      → every descendant (pgrep), so a backgrounded dev server shows
  lsof         → TCP ports it LISTENs on, and who it talks to (outbound)
⚠ marks a settled agent (idle/done) still holding a LISTEN port or burning CPU
in a child — the "sleeping sheep left something running" case. Read-only.
```

### pasture agent stop

Stop an agent without waiting for it to cooperate — graceful, then forced

- **Safety:** `external`
- **Usage:** `pasture agent stop <pane> [--force] [--yes] [--timeout SECONDS]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/agent/stop`](../cmds/agent/stop)

```text
A control action over the flock, so it is HUMAN-gated: it prints its plan and
does nothing without --yes. An agent must not stop another agent on its own —
a looping or hostile one could silence its reviewer or clear its rivals (same
rule as "never answer another agent's approval dialog for the user").

Escalation, so a wedged or ignoring agent still dies:
  1. graceful — send the agent's own quit (/exit, /quit) and wait --timeout
     (default 10s) for its process to leave. A courtesy with a deadline.
  2. herdr pane close — herdr ends the pane's process tree.
  3. kill -TERM the whole process set, then -KILL any survivor.
--force skips step 1 (straight to pane close + kill). Sending a quit command
is not answering an approval dialog; if the agent is blocked, step 1 simply
fails and we escalate — we never click through its dialog.
```

### pasture agent sweep

Free memory — send idle agents home, keep a ledger to call them back

- **Safety:** `external`
- **Usage:** `pasture agent sweep [--yes] [--force] [--close] [--include-named] [--timeout S] | --tidy [--yes] | --recall`
- **Source:** [`cmds/agent/sweep`](../cmds/agent/sweep)

```text
Idle agents hold hundreds of MB each; a few dozen push a 16GB Mac into swap
while the CPU sits idle. Their sessions are saved on quit, so sending them
home is cheap: call one back when you need it (`--recall` prints how).

Picks agents that are `idle` only. Never `done` (an answer you have not read),
`working` or `blocked`. Also skipped: the pane running this, the focused pane,
and named agents (pasture-duo reviewers idle between rounds) unless
--include-named.

HUMAN-gated like `pasture agent stop`: prints the plan, does nothing without
--yes (exit 3). Not for an agent to call on the flock by itself.

  1. writes each one to the ledger ~/.cache/pasture/swept.tsv
  2. sends every agent its own quit (/exit, /quit) at once, waits --timeout
     (default 8s)
  3. survivors: listed — or, with --force, handed to `pasture agent stop
     --force` (pane close, then signals). Grok tends to ignore /quit.
  4. --close: closes the tabs those agents sat in — only a tab whose every
     pane is now a bare shell (or lazygit) with no background job. A tab
     that still runs hx, a dev server, a build or another agent is kept and
     named. A workspace left with nothing but closable tabs is closed whole.
     The ledger keeps each agent's directory, so --recall still works.

--tidy closes every such idle tab without quitting any agent (for tabs a
sweep without --close left behind). Never the focused tab or this one.
```

## dep

### pasture dep audit

Scan this repo offline for secrets, SAST issues, and vulnerable deps

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture dep audit [--history] [--fail-on LEVEL] [--json]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/dep/audit`](../cmds/dep/audit)

```text
Runs the offline scanners the security-analysis / dependency-management skills
teach, over the current repo, and skips any tool that is not installed. No
code ever leaves the machine (grype needs one `grype db update` beforehand,
then runs offline; semgrep fetches its ruleset once, then caches it).
  gitleaks  secrets — working tree, or the full git history with --history
  semgrep   SAST (p/default); exit told apart from a ruleset-fetch failure
  grype     known-CVE dependencies, catalogued from lockfiles via syft
One line per tool, then a summary. Exit 1 if any tool reports a finding,
5 if not one scanner is installed. --fail-on sets grype's severity gate
(default high): negligible|low|medium|high|critical.
```

### pasture dep cve

Look up one dependency or CVE: is this lib vulnerable, how risky is this CVE

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture dep cve <purl|CVE-ID> [--json]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/dep/cve`](../cmds/dep/cve)

```text
Two modes, both read-only HTTP to public advisory APIs. Only the purl or the
CVE id leaves the machine — never your code.
  pkg:...    query OSV.dev for vulns affecting that exact package version
  CVE-xxxx   EPSS exploit-probability (FIRST) + CISA KEV known-exploited check
purl form: pkg:<type>/<namespace>/<name>@<version>, e.g.
  pkg:maven/io.vertx/vertx-core@4.4.0    pkg:npm/lodash@4.17.20
```

## doc

### pasture doc review

Fresh-eyes review of a doc — each reviewer a NEW headless agent (no shared context), several vendors

- **Safety:** `external`
- **Usage:** `pasture doc review <file> [--yes] [--vendors claude,codex,grok] [--personas a,b] [--jobs N] [--timeout S] [--dry-run]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/doc/review`](../cmds/doc/review)

```text
"Goldfish" review (after the Elephant-Goldfish Model, egm.dev): the author's
own agent carries the conversation that produced the doc, so it validates its
own assumptions. Here every (persona × vendor) pair is a brand-new headless
process that gets only the doc's path and a persona brief — zero context by
construction, not by instruction — and different vendors bring different
blind spots. Personas live in cmds/doc/personas/.

Each reviewer runs under a macOS Seatbelt profile (sandbox-exec): it cannot
read or write anything in $HOME except reading the tree under review and its
own login file — no transcripts, memory, skills or MCP config — so a doc that tries to talk it into reading
~/.ssh or another repo gets "Operation not permitted". On top of that:
  claude  cwd = empty temp dir, repo via --add-dir; user settings, hooks,
          plugins, MCP servers, skills and auto-memory off; tools Read/Grep/
          Glob only. (The login's account email is still in its context.)
  codex   no tools at all (shell, browser, computer use, apps, plugins,
          hooks off; its own sandbox cannot nest in ours): the doc goes in
          the prompt and codex reviews the doc alone, never the code.
  grok    plan mode, no web search, and only its read_file/list_dir/grep
          tools (by default it also has X search, a terminal and image
          generation); it runs with cwd = the tree under review.

The doc — and whatever the reviewers read — LEAVES THE MACHINE to every vendor
used. So what they may see, and who may see it:
  public repo, doc pushed unchanged → reviewers get a `git archive` snapshot
      of origin's default branch: only what is already public, never your
      untracked files or drafts. Vendors: claude, codex, grok.
  any other repo, or a public repo's unpushed/changed doc → the real working
      tree, and only $PASTURE_PRIVATE_REVIEW_VENDORS (default: claude).
  not in a git repo → a temp dir holding a copy of the doc alone (never its
      parent directory, which may be $HOME); same private vendors.
Asking for a vendor the policy refuses exits 3 — widen it yourself, knowing
your employer's rules; an agent must not widen it for you. Human-gated like
every external command: prints its plan, does nothing without --yes.

Findings: every reviewer must answer in lines of
  FINDING: <blocker|major|minor> | <where> | <problem> | <fix>
They are collected, tagged persona/vendor and sorted by severity. Raw answers
stay in the run directory printed at the end.
```

## flow

### pasture flow board

SDLC pipeline board — what lifecycle stage every agent's task sits at

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture flow board [--no-pr] [--json]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/flow/board`](../cmds/flow/board)

```text
pasture runs tasks in parallel (one agent, one worktree, one branch), so "what
stage is each task at" is scattered across herdr, git and the forge. This
joins them into one pipeline view. Per task (an agent's worktree) it infers a
stage from signals the task did not have to report:

  🌱 spawned      worktree + agent, no commit yet
  ⌨️  coding        commits not pushed, or a dirty tree, or agent working
  📤 review-ready  pushed, no PR open yet
  👀 in-review     PR open, awaiting review
  🔧 changes       PR open, changes requested
  🔁 ci            PR open, checks running or failing
  ✅ mergeable     PR open, approved + checks green
  🔀 merged        PR merged (worktree can be swept: pasture-task --done)
  ⛔ blocked       agent waiting on you (overlaid on its stage)

PR data comes from `gh` per GitHub repo (one call each, in parallel). --no-pr
skips the network and shows only the local stages. Read-only.
```

## git

### pasture git guard

Pre-push gate — block a push to a PUBLIC remote that carries a secret

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture git guard <remote-name> <remote-url>   (reads git pre-push stdin)`
- **Source:** [`cmds/git/guard`](../cmds/git/guard)

```text
Written to be a git pre-push hook body (`pasture git protect` installs it).
Reads the ref lines git feeds a pre-push hook on stdin, finds the commits
being pushed, and runs gitleaks over just those commits:
  public remote        → a secret BLOCKS the push (exit 1)
  private / internal   → a secret only warns; the push proceeds
Visibility comes from `pasture git visibility`. When the forge can't answer
(unknown), the push is BLOCKED by default — fail closed — unless the host is
on the user-local internal allowlist (one host per line in
~/.config/pasture/internal-hosts, or $PASTURE_INTERNAL_HOSTS, space/comma
separated). That is the only way a host reads as internal without the forge
confirming it, so a mis-cased host, an ssh alias, or an unknown public host
cannot silently pass. Override a real block the human way:
  git push --no-verify   — an agent must not do this on the user's behalf.
```

### pasture git protect

Install the pre-push secret guard into this repo (keeps any existing hook)

- **Safety:** `write`
- **Usage:** `pasture git protect [--remove]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/git/protect`](../cmds/git/protect)

```text
Writes a pre-push hook into THIS repo's hooks dir that runs `pasture git
guard` (block a secret pushed to a public remote). An existing pre-push hook
is preserved as pre-push.local and chained, so husky/lefthook still run.
Scoped to one repo: no global core.hooksPath, so other repos are untouched.
--remove restores the previous hook (or deletes ours).
```

### pasture git visibility

Ask the forge whether a git remote is public, private, or internal

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture git visibility [remote|url]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/git/visibility`](../cmds/git/visibility)

```text
Resolves <remote> (default origin) to its URL, or takes a URL directly, then
asks the forge: gh for github.com, glab for a GitLab host. Prints one word:
  public | private | internal | unknown
unknown means the forge could not answer (host not github/gitlab, CLI missing
or unauthed, or the call failed). A caller decides what unknown means for it;
`pasture git guard` treats unknown as public only on the public SaaS hosts.
```

## mr

### pasture mr fanout

Move stacked branches off the branch below them and onto the default branch (trunk-based)

- **Safety:** `external`
- **Usage:** `pasture mr fanout <branch>... [--onto BRANCH] [--yes]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/mr/fanout`](../cmds/mr/fanout)

```text
For each <branch> (a remote branch, e.g. one MR of a stack), finds the branch
it is stacked on and replays only its own commits onto --onto (default: the
default branch), then force-pushes it with a lease. Use it for independent
parts once what they really need (a shared library, say) has merged: each MR
then shows only its own diff and can merge on its own.

Without --yes it prints the plan and changes nothing. Rebases run in a
temporary worktree, so your checkout is untouched. A conflict aborts that
branch and leaves it as it was. You still own building and testing the
result: moving a branch off a dependency it really needs breaks it.
```

### pasture mr stack

Show open merge requests as a stack: what sits on what, own vs cumulative diff, CI

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture mr stack <search> [--label LABEL] [--json]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/mr/stack`](../cmds/mr/stack)

```text
GitLab, through glab, in the current repo. Finds open MRs whose title or
description matches <search> (a ticket id works), or carrying --label, then
for each source branch works out which other branch it is stacked on.
Flags MRs that sit on another branch yet target the default branch: their
diff includes everything below them (review it once, merge it in order, or
retarget / `pasture mr fanout` the independent ones).
```

## pane

### pasture pane tail

Read another pane's recent output, or wait until a pattern shows up

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture pane tail <pane> [--lines N] [--wait REGEX] [--timeout SECONDS]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/pane/tail`](../cmds/pane/tail)

```text
<pane> is a herdr pane id (herdr pane list). --wait blocks until REGEX
appears in the pane (a dev server's "ready", a test's "FAIL"), then prints
the last --lines lines (default 80). Exit 4 if the wait times out.
```

## repo

### pasture repo who

Which agents stand in which worktree of this repo — look before you code here

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture repo who [dir] [--check] [--json]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/repo/who`](../cmds/repo/who)

```text
git locks a branch to one worktree, but not a directory: a second agent can
still cd into a worktree another agent is editing. This lists every worktree
of the repo that holds [dir] (default: here) with its branch, uncommitted file
count, and the herdr agents whose directory is inside it. ⚠ marks a worktree
with two or more agents in it.

--check is for an agent about to edit: exit 3 when another agent (not this
pane) is in the same worktree as [dir], 0 when it is free. Make your own
worktree then (pasture-task <branch>) instead of working beside it.
```

## sec

### pasture sec pentest

Pentest your own code or local app with Strix AI agents, inside its Docker sandbox

- **Safety:** `external`
- **Usage:** `pasture sec pentest <dir|file|url>... [--mode quick|standard|deep] [--budget USD] [--instruction TEXT] [--yes]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/sec/pentest`](../cmds/sec/pentest)

```text
Strix (github.com/usestrix/strix) runs a team of AI agents in a Docker
sandbox that read the code, run the app and try real exploits. It ATTACKS the
targets and sends what it sees to an LLM, so this wrapper decides three things
before it runs, and prints them as a plan:

  what it may attack
    dir / file   a code target. Strix mounts targets writable, so it gets a
                 copy in the run directory, never your checkout: the files git
                 tracks plus untracked ones not ignored (.env and other
                 ignored secrets stay out). A dir must be inside a git repo.
    URL / host   loopback only (localhost, 127.x, ::1,
                 host.docker.internal) — unless the host is listed in
                 ~/.config/pasture/pentest-scope, one per line. Only list a
                 host you own or have WRITTEN permission to test. That file is
                 the human's to write; an agent must never add to it.
    a git URL    refused: clone it and pass the directory.

  which LLM may see it ($STRIX_LLM, or the one Strix saved in
  ~/.strix/cli-config.json; its prefix is the provider)
    a public repo, clean and with HEAD on origin, alone → any provider: what
      is sent is already public.
    anything else (private code, unpushed work, any URL) → only a provider in
      $PASTURE_PRIVATE_PENTEST_PROVIDERS (default: anthropic), or a local model
      (ollama, lm_studio, or $LLM_API_BASE on loopback). Widening the list is
      the human's call, knowing their employer's rules.

  how much  --mode (default quick) and --budget (default 5 USD, Strix's own
    --max-budget). Never `strix cloud`: nothing is uploaded to strix.ai.

Human-gated: without --yes it prints the plan and exits 3. Results and the
full report stay in the run directory printed at the end. Exit 0 no
findings, 1 findings or Strix failed, 3 refused or needs --yes, 5 missing
tool (strix, docker) or Docker not running.
```

## stack

### pasture stack attach

Put git's HEAD back on this worktree's branch after Sapling detached it

- **Safety:** `write`
- **Usage:** `pasture stack attach [--branch B] [--dry-run] [--quiet]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/stack/attach`](../cmds/stack/attach)

```text
`sl prev`, `sl next` and `sl goto` leave git's HEAD detached (a plain
`sl commit` on an attached HEAD does not). Detached, the worktree no longer
holds its branch: git's "one branch, one worktree" lock is gone, so another
worktree can check the branch out, and `wt list` / `pasture-task --done` stop
finding the task. This puts HEAD back on the branch, without touching files:
  HEAD is the branch's tip            → attach (same commit, nothing changes)
  HEAD is ahead of it (commits made   → move the branch up to HEAD
    on top while detached)              (a fast-forward), then attach
  HEAD is below it (mid-stack)        → nothing yet: `sl top`, then attach
  HEAD and the branch have diverged   → nothing: look first (exit 3)

Which branch: --branch, else the one recorded for this worktree (pasture-task
records it; so does this command whenever it finds HEAD attached), else the
only local branch at HEAD that no other worktree has checked out.
--quiet prints nothing and always exits 0 — for the Sapling hooks in
pasture's sapling.conf, which run it after sl goto/next/prev.
```

### pasture stack push

Push each commit of the current Sapling stack to its own branch, optionally as a chain of MRs

- **Safety:** `external`
- **Usage:** `pasture stack push <branch-prefix> [--mr] [--base BRANCH] [--yes]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/stack/push`](../cmds/stack/push)

```text
Run in a repo where the stack was built with `sl` (see `sl stack`). Commit n
of the stack, bottom first, goes to branch <prefix>-<n>-<slug of its title>.
Rerun after `sl amend` / `sl absorb`: branches that changed are force-pushed,
with a lease on the remote commit the plan showed — if someone pushed to the
branch since, the push is refused instead of overwriting their work.
--mr also opens a GitLab merge request per branch with glab, each targeting
the branch below it (the first targets --base, default the default branch),
or fixes the target of an existing one.

Without --yes it prints the plan and changes nothing.
```

## sys

### pasture sys line

One-line machine load + memory metric with trend sparklines (for a status line)

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture sys line [--width N] [--load-only|--mem-only] [--plain] [--reset]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/sys/line`](../cmds/sys/line)

```text
Prints a compact, pollable line meant for herdr's tab_bar_right (type =
"command") or any status bar / prompt:

    load 1.3× ▂▃▅▇  mem 61% ▃▄▆█

load  = 1-minute load average ÷ CPU count, as a ratio. 1.0× means the run
        queue equals the core count (cores full); >1 means oversubscribed —
        the signal that matters while running several agents and builds.
        Read from sysctl, so each poll costs ~0ms and spawns nothing (unlike
        `top`/`iostat`, which would add load just to measure it).
mem   = (active + wired + compressor) pages ÷ total RAM. Reclaimable pages
        (inactive, speculative, purgeable, free) count as available, so this
        tracks real pressure / swap risk, not Activity Monitor's "used".

The sparkline is the recent trend: each run appends one sample to a tiny ring
buffer under ${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/pasture and renders the last --width
of them (default 12). load scales to its own recent range (trend shape); mem
scales 0–100%. Plain text only (no ANSI), so a tab bar renders it verbatim.
```

## web

### pasture web read

Read a web page as text: plain fetch first, a real browser when that fails

- **Safety:** `read`
- **Usage:** `pasture web read <url> [--browser] [--max-chars N]`
- **Source:** [`cmds/web/read`](../cmds/web/read)

```text
The fetch (curl + macOS textutil) is fast and cheap. It falls back to
agent-browser, which runs JavaScript, when the fetch errors or returns a page
that is nearly empty or a JS/bot wall. --browser skips the fetch. Output is
cut at --max-chars (default 20000). The first line says which way was used.

This is a `read` command agents run freely, so the browser it falls back to
is never your logged-in one: a fresh agent-browser session per call, closed
afterwards, with every AGENT_BROWSER_* variable (profile, args, extensions,
executable…) removed from its environment and an empty --config in place of
~/.agent-browser/config.json. Pages that need your login are
for `agent-browser --profile …` directly, which you choose to run.
```
